unit.title: Plan to undertake a routine task

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: What is a routine task?
options: A task that is new and has never been done before
A task done only in an emergency
A task done often, in the same usual way
A task that needs no planning at all

questions.stem: Where should you look first to find out exactly what a job needs?
options: The job card or work order for the task
A friend who once did a different job
The price list in the hardware shop
The weather report for the coming week

questions.stem: Your supervisor gives you a job by phone, and you are not sure of one detail. What should you do?
options: Guess, and fix it later if it turns out wrong
Wait until next week before starting the job
Ask the customer what they think it means
Ask the supervisor and write the answer down

questions.stem: A work order says: 'Replace faulty outlet, Unit 4, by 2 p.m.' Which three facts does it give?
options: The cost, the colour and the make
The task, the place and the deadline
The tools, the weather and the price
The customer's name, age and phone

questions.stem: Why should you read all the instructions before you start a task?
options: So that you can say you have read them
So you know the whole job before you begin
So you can tell the others they are wrong
So that you will not need any of the tools

questions.stem: What is a specification?
options: A list of all the workers' phone numbers and names
A drawing that shows only the site entrance
A note of the time each worker arrives on site
A document giving the materials and quality needed

questions.stem: Who should you check with if the drawing and the job card do not agree?
options: Your supervisor
The delivery driver
A passer-by on the road
No one; just choose one

questions.stem: What does 'quality standard' mean for a task?
options: How fast the worker can do the job
How many tools are used on the job
How well the finished work must be done
How much the customer will pay for it

questions.stem: Which document tells you how to use and look after a power tool?
options: The maker's instruction manual
The site's delivery notes for it
The customer's invoice for the tool
The weekly time sheet for the site

questions.stem: On a drawing, where do you find the meaning of the symbols?
options: In the title block only
On the back of the job card
In the legend (key)
In the scale bar

questions.stem: Why must you check that you have the latest version of a drawing?
options: Older drawings are much easier to read
The design may have changed since then
Newer drawings are always printed in colour
Old drawings show the price of the materials

questions.stem: What is a safe work procedure?
options: A list of the tools kept in the store
A note of when to take your breaks
A list of the customer's wishes for the job
Written steps for doing a task safely

questions.stem: Where can you find the rules for working safely at the Centre?
options: In the hardware shop's latest price list
On the back of the materials invoice
In an old drawing of a different job site
In the Centre's safety rules and procedures

questions.stem: Why is it useful to break a task into steps?
options: It makes the task take much longer to do
It helps you work in order and miss nothing
It means that you need fewer tools and materials
It stops the need for any safety checks

questions.stem: Which is the best order of work for replacing a light switch?
options: Remove old switch, isolate and prove dead, fit new, test
Fit new switch, remove old one, isolate and prove dead, test
Isolate and prove dead, remove old switch, fit new, test
Test, fit new switch, isolate and prove dead, remove old

questions.stem: Why should you plan where to put tools and materials before you start?
options: So they are at hand and out of walkways
So you can carry more of them at one time
So the customer can see how many you have
So that they can be left there after the job

questions.stem: Andre has three small jobs in one building. How should he plan them?
options: Do the hardest job last, whatever happens
Put them in a sensible order to save trips
Do all three at the same time, bit by bit
Start each one and leave it to start the next

questions.stem: What is a method statement?
options: Written steps saying how a job will be done
A list of payments made to the workers
The receipt for materials bought for a job
A letter telling a customer the job is late

questions.stem: Why should a plan include checks during the work, and not only at the end?
options: So the job takes more time and costs more
So that more materials can be used up
So faults are found early and fixed easily
So that you can stop for longer breaks

questions.stem: Which is the first step in planning a routine task?
options: Start work and plan as you go
Order all the materials at once
Clean up the work area
Find out what the task needs

questions.stem: Why should you make a materials list before you start a job?
options: So that you can buy extra items for yourself
To make the job look bigger to the customer
So you have what you need and save trips
So that you do not need to read the drawing

questions.stem: Before a task, why do you check that the tools you need are in good condition?
options: So that you can sell the old ones on
So the toolbox weighs a little less
So that the customer will like them
So the work is safe and is not held up

questions.stem: A job needs 12 m of cable. You allow about 10% extra for connections and waste. How much should you take?
options: About 13 m
About 10 m
About 24 m
About 12 m

questions.stem: A material you need is out of stock. Who should you tell?
options: Nobody; just use something else instead
Your supervisor, so the plan can change
Only the other trainees in your group
The customer's next-door neighbour

questions.stem: When a task needs two people, what should the plan show?
options: Who does each part, and when
Only the name of the leader
Which person is paid the most
Nothing about the people at all

questions.stem: Why should you check the materials delivered against the materials list?
options: To see if the delivery van is clean inside
To be sure the right items and amounts came
To count how many of the boxes are blue
To note the time of the delivery only

questions.stem: Besides tools and materials, which resources must be planned for most tasks?
options: The colour of the work van
The make of each worker's phone
The size of the car park
The time and the people needed

questions.stem: Why do you look for hazards while planning a task, and not after you start?
options: So you can tell the customer about them later
So that the job will become more interesting
So controls are ready before anyone is at risk
So that fewer workers are needed on the job

questions.stem: Your task is to change a ceiling light fitting. Which hazards should your plan deal with first?
options: Dust lying on top of the old fitting
The colour and style of the new fitting
The cost of the new fitting and lamps
Electric shock and working at height

questions.stem: Which control must be in the plan for any work on an electrical circuit?
options: Work quickly to keep the time short
Wear thick gloves so you can work on it live
Isolate, lock off, tag and prove dead
Work only when the customer is out

questions.stem: What is a risk assessment?
options: A list of the prices of all the materials used
A check of what may cause harm and its controls
A report on how fast the job was finished
A form that the customer signs to pay for it

questions.stem: Why should the plan say which PPE is needed for the task?
options: So it is ready and worn when the work starts
So it can be bought after the job is done
So the customer can try it on before you
So it can be left behind safely in the van

questions.stem: You will work in an office while staff are there. What should your plan include?
options: Starting work before you tell anyone there
Telling the people there and keeping them clear
Leaving tools out on the desks at lunch time
Turning off all the power without any warning

questions.stem: Why should a plan include a time estimate for each step?
options: So that the worker can always leave early
So that every break can be made a bit longer
So the customer can be charged by the minute
So the job finishes on time and others can plan

questions.stem: A task has 4 steps of 30 minutes each and a 15-minute clean-up. How long should you plan for?
options: 2 hours 15 minutes
1 hour 45 minutes
2 hours
3 hours 15 minutes

questions.stem: You find that the job will take longer than planned. What should you do?
options: Rush the rest of the work to catch up
Leave out the testing to save some time
Tell your supervisor as soon as you know
Stop work and go home early for the day

questions.stem: Which is the best way to show the order and timing of the steps of a job?
options: A shopping list of items
A photo of the work site
A simple work schedule
A copy of the last receipt

questions.stem: Why should you go over your plan with your supervisor before starting?
options: To check it and agree on any changes
To get the supervisor to do the work
To make the plan longer and more detailed
To be paid before the job is started

questions.stem: During a task, the customer asks you to add an extra outlet. What should you do?
options: Fit it at once without telling anyone at all
Refuse, and say that it is not possible
Fit it and charge the customer double later
Note it and check with your supervisor first

questions.stem: Why should you check the finished work against the job card?
options: To see how many lines the card has on it
To make sure all that was asked is done
To change the card so it matches the work
To find the price that will be charged

questions.stem: After a task, what should you do if part of your plan did not work well?
options: Note it so the plan can be improved next time
Forget about it and move on to the next one
Blame another worker in the group for it
Throw the plan away and never use it again

questions.stem: Which is the clearest way to give a co-worker instructions for their part of a task?
options: Shout them across the site while working
Explain clearly and check they understand
Send a text message after they have started
Let them work it out by themselves

questions.stem: When a routine task is finished, what should you do with the work area?
options: Leave it for the next worker to clean
Clean only the parts the customer can see
Clean up, remove waste and return tools
Lock it up with the waste still inside

questions.stem: What should a completion report for a task include?
options: Only the name of the worker who did it
Only the time that the job was finished
Only the price that will be charged for it
What was done, any problems, and results

questions.stem: You find a fault that is outside the job you were given. What should you do?
options: Fix it without telling anyone
Ignore it, as it is not your job
Tell the customer it is their fault
Report it to your supervisor

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What is the name of the document that tells a worker which job to do, where to do it, and by when?
What is the name of the box on a drawing that shows its title, drawing number, scale and date?
What do the letters PPE stand for?
A task has three steps that take 20, 40 and 30 minutes. How many minutes is that in total?
What is the name of the scale drawing that shows, from above, where things go in a building?
One box holds 100 cable clips and a job needs 250 clips. How many boxes must you order?
What is the name of the short meeting at the start of a shift where the team goes over the day's tasks and hazards?
What do we call the latest date or time by which a task must be finished?
What do we call anything that could cause harm, such as a live cable or a wet floor?
What job title is usually given to the person at work who gives you your tasks and checks your work?
On a drawing with a scale of 1:100, a cable run measures 50 mm. How long is it in real life, in metres?
What is the name of the list of items needed for a job, with the amount of each?
What one word means the order in which the steps of a task must be done?
What do we call a written list of items that is ticked off one by one so nothing is missed?
What is the name of the check, done by looking carefully, before you use a tool?

essays.stem: Describe the steps you would follow to plan a routine task, from the moment you receive the work order until you are ready to start.
essays.modelAnswer: First I read the work order or job card carefully to find out what the task is, where it is, when it must be finished and what standard is needed. If anything is unclear, I ask my supervisor and write down the answer. Next I collect the information I need, such as the drawing, the specification, the maker's instructions and the Centre's safe work procedures. I then break the task into steps and put them in a sensible order, with checks along the way. I make a list of the tools, materials and people needed, and check that they are available and in good condition. I look for hazards, such as electric shock or working at height, and plan the controls, including safe isolation. I estimate the time for each step. Finally I go over the plan with my supervisor, agree any changes and tell the people who will be affected.
markingPoints: Reads the work order and finds the task, place, deadline and standard; asks if unclear
Collects information: drawings, specifications, maker's instructions, procedures
Breaks the task into steps in a sensible order with checks
Lists and checks tools, materials and people; identifies hazards and controls
Estimates time and agrees the plan with the supervisor

essays.stem: Name the sources of information you would use to plan a task and explain what each one tells you.
essays.modelAnswer: The job card or work order tells me what the task is, where it is, who asked for it and when it must be finished. The drawings show where the work goes, with symbols explained in the legend and a scale to work out real sizes. The specification tells me which materials to use and the standard the finished work must meet. The maker's instructions tell me how to fit and use equipment and tools safely and correctly. The Centre's safety rules and safe work procedures tell me the safe way to do the job, such as how to isolate a circuit. My supervisor can answer questions and tell me about any changes, and the customer or building user can tell me about access and times when work can be done. I always check that I have the latest version of each document.
markingPoints: Job card or work order: the task, place and deadline
Drawings: where the work goes, with legend and scale
Specification: materials and quality standard
Maker's instructions and safe work procedures: correct and safe methods
Supervisor or customer for questions and access; checks for the latest version

essays.stem: Write a step-by-step plan for replacing a faulty socket outlet in an office at the Centre.
essays.modelAnswer: 1. Read the job card and check which outlet is faulty and when the work can be done. 2. Tell the office staff that the outlet and its circuit will be off, and ask them to save their work and unplug their equipment. 3. Collect the tools and materials: a new outlet of the same type, screwdrivers, a voltage tester and proving unit, a lock and tag, and PPE. 4. Find the circuit on the board chart, switch it off, lock it off and tag it. 5. Check the tester on the proving unit, prove the outlet dead between all conductors, and check the tester again. 6. Remove the old outlet, noting where each conductor goes. 7. Fit the new outlet, with tight terminals and the earth connected. 8. Fix the outlet straight and fit the cover. 9. Have the outlet tested as the Centre's rules say, remove my lock and restore the supply, and check that the outlet works. 10. Clean up, tell the staff and report the job as complete.
markingPoints: Reads the job card and informs the people affected
Lists the correct tools, materials and PPE
Includes full safe isolation: switch off, lock off, tag, prove dead with a tester checked before and after
Removes and fits the outlet in a sensible order with earth connected and terminals tight
Includes testing, restoring the supply, cleaning up and reporting

essays.stem: Explain how you would identify the hazards of a routine task and plan how to control them.
essays.modelAnswer: Before the task, I look at each step of the plan and ask what could go wrong and who could be hurt. I visit the work area if I can, and I read the safe work procedure and the maker's instructions. I look for hazards such as live conductors, working at height, power tools, dust, trip hazards and other people walking nearby. For each hazard I decide how likely it is to cause harm and how bad the harm could be. Then I choose controls, starting with the best: remove the hazard if I can, for example by isolating the circuit and proving it dead; then use safer equipment, such as a fibreglass stepladder; then put up barriers and signs and agree safe working times; and finally wear the right PPE. I write the hazards and controls on a risk assessment and go through it with my supervisor and the team before starting.
markingPoints: Looks at each step and asks what could go wrong and who could be hurt
Gives suitable hazards for the task (electricity, height, tools, trips, other people)
Considers how likely and how serious the harm would be
Chooses controls in a sensible order, with isolation for electrical work and PPE last
Writes them on a risk assessment and shares it before starting

essays.stem: Explain how you would work out what tools and materials a task needs, and how you would check them before you start.
essays.modelAnswer: I start with the job card, the drawing and the specification. From the drawing I count the items, such as outlets, switches and boxes, and use the scale to work out the lengths of cable and conduit. I add a little extra, about ten per cent, for connections and waste. I write a materials list with the type, size and amount of each item. For the tools, I go through each step of the plan and write down the tools and test instruments needed, including PPE and the lock and tag for isolation. Before I start, I check the materials against the list to make sure the right items and amounts have come and that nothing is damaged. I check each tool and instrument for damage and make sure testers work on a proving unit. Anything missing or faulty is reported to my supervisor so that the plan can be changed in time.
markingPoints: Uses the job card, drawing and specification
Counts items and uses the scale to work out lengths, adding a little extra
Writes a materials list with type, size and amount; lists tools by going through each step
Checks delivered materials against the list for the right items, amounts and condition
Checks tools and instruments before use and reports anything missing or faulty

essays.stem: Explain why a time estimate and a simple schedule are important when planning a task, and describe how you would make one.
essays.modelAnswer: A time estimate tells everyone how long the job should take. It helps the supervisor plan other work, lets the customer know when the power will be off, and shows if the job can be finished by the deadline. A schedule shows the order of the steps and when each one will be done, so the team knows what comes next. To make one, I list the steps of the task in order. For each step I estimate how long it will take, using past jobs and asking more experienced workers. I add time for setting up, safe isolation, testing and cleaning up, which are easy to forget, and a little extra for problems. I add up the times to get the total. I then draw a simple table or bar chart showing each step and its start and finish time. During the job I compare progress with the schedule and tell my supervisor early if it is slipping.
markingPoints: Explains why: meets the deadline, helps others plan, tells the customer when power is off
Lists the steps in order and estimates each one from experience or advice
Includes setting up, isolation, testing, cleaning up and some extra time
Adds the times and shows them in a simple table or chart
Checks progress against the schedule and reports delays early

essays.stem: Explain who you need to tell about your plan for a routine task, and what each of them needs to know.
essays.modelAnswer: My supervisor needs to see the plan before I start, so that they can check it is correct and safe, agree the method and time, and tell me about anything I do not know, such as other work in the area. My team members need to know the steps, who does each part, the hazards and controls, and the PPE to wear; a short toolbox talk is a good way to share this, and I check that they understand. The customer or the people who use the building need to know when the work will happen, which areas or circuits will be off and for how long, and what they must do, such as saving computer work or keeping clear of the area. If the task affects other trades on site, they also need to know. I give information clearly, in plain words, and I write down any changes we agree.
markingPoints: Supervisor: checks and agrees the plan, method and time
Team: steps, roles, hazards, controls and PPE, for example in a toolbox talk
Customer or building users: when, what will be off, how long, and what they must do
Other trades affected are told
Speaks clearly, checks understanding and records agreed changes

essays.stem: Describe what you should do if something changes or goes wrong while you are carrying out a planned task.
essays.modelAnswer: If something changes, such as finding a fault that was not expected, missing materials, damaged equipment or a delay, I first make sure the work area is safe. If the problem affects safety, I stop work, leave the circuit isolated and locked off, and keep other people away. I do not guess or take short cuts, such as leaving out a test to save time. I tell my supervisor straight away and explain clearly what I found. We agree what to do: for example, change the order of the steps, get other materials, or arrange another visit. I update the plan and the time estimate and tell the team and the customer about the change. I write the change and the reason on the job card or in my notes, so there is a record. After the job, I note what happened so that future plans can allow for it.
markingPoints: Makes the area safe first; stops work if safety is affected, keeping the circuit isolated
Does not take short cuts or guess
Tells the supervisor at once and agrees what to do
Updates the plan and tells the team and customer
Records the change and uses it to improve future plans

essays.stem: Explain how you would check the quality of finished work against the plan and the specification.
essays.modelAnswer: When the work is finished, I compare it with the job card to make sure every item asked for has been done. I check it against the drawing to see that each outlet, switch or fitting is in the right place and at the right height. I check it against the specification to see that the right materials and fittings were used. I look at the workmanship: accessories fixed firmly and straight, covers fitted, cables neatly run and fixed, no bare copper showing, and no damage to the walls or the customer's property. I make sure the required tests have been done and passed, and that the results are recorded. If I find anything wrong, I put it right before handing over, or I report it to my supervisor if I cannot. Finally I ask the supervisor to inspect the work and sign it off.
markingPoints: Checks every item on the job card has been done
Checks positions against the drawing and materials against the specification
Checks workmanship: firm, straight, neat, covers on, no bare copper, no damage
Makes sure tests are done, passed and recorded
Fixes or reports faults and has the supervisor sign off the work

essays.stem: Describe how you would finish a routine task and explain why reviewing the plan afterwards is useful.
essays.modelAnswer: To finish the task, I make sure the work has been checked and tested and that the supervisor is happy with it. I clean the work area, remove off-cuts and packaging, and put waste in the right bins. I check my tools and count them so none are left behind in a board or ceiling, and I return them clean to the store. Any unused materials go back to the store and are booked in. I tell the customer or the building users that the work is done and explain anything they need to know. I complete the job card or completion report, writing what was done, the materials used, the test results, the time taken and any problems found. Reviewing the plan afterwards is useful because I can compare what happened with what I planned. I can see which time estimates were wrong or what was missed, and use this to make better plans next time.
markingPoints: Has the work checked and approved
Cleans up, sorts waste, and counts and returns tools and unused materials
Tells the customer or users that the work is complete
Completes the job card or report with what was done, materials, results, time and problems
Explains that reviewing the plan shows what went wrong and improves future plans

practical1.title: Write a full work plan for a routine electrical task from a job card
practical1.brief: As a group, write a complete work plan for one routine task. The assessor gives each group a job card, a layout drawing to scale and the maker's sheet for the fitting, for one of these tasks: (a) add two new socket outlets in the Centre's training office, fed from an existing circuit, or (b) replace four old ceiling light fittings in a classroom with new LED batten fittings. Nothing is installed in this task. Each member writes one section of the plan and then reads it out to the group, who check it: (1) the task: what, where, by when and to what standard, with any questions for the supervisor, (2) the steps in order, including safe isolation (switch off, lock off and tag, prove dead with a tester checked before and after) and the checks along the way, (3) the materials list, with lengths worked out from the drawing's scale plus about 10% extra, and the tools and test instruments list, (4) the risk assessment, with each hazard and its control, (5) the time schedule, as a simple bar chart, and who does each step. In a group of 4, sections 4 and 5 are shared by two members. The group then presents the plan to the assessor, playing the supervisor, and agrees any changes. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in the finished plan once for the whole group.
materials: A job card, a layout drawing to scale and the maker's sheet for the fitting (from the assessor)
Planning sheets: task summary, step list, materials and tools list, risk assessment form, schedule chart
Rulers, pencils, a calculator and a scale rule
A phone or camera for the photos
photos: The group reading the job card and drawing together
The task summary and the list of questions for the supervisor
The step list, with the safe isolation steps shown
The materials and tools list, with the scale working shown
The time schedule chart showing who does each step
The group presenting the plan to the assessor
checklist: Read the job card and drawing and picked out the task, place, deadline and standard
Wrote their own section clearly and accurately
Put the steps in a safe and sensible order, with safe isolation in full
Worked out lengths from the scale correctly and added sensible extra
Listed hazards with suitable controls on the risk assessment
Gave realistic times and showed who does each step
Checked another member's section and suggested corrections
Explained their section clearly to the assessor and agreed changes
safety: No tools or electrical equipment are used in this task; keep the planning area tidy and bags off the floor
The plan must show full safe isolation for any electrical work, and must never plan live work
Plan for working at height with a suitable non-conducting stepladder, as the Centre's rules say
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules in every part of the plan

practical2.title: Plan and carry out a routine task on a practice board, then complete a job report
practical2.brief: As a group, plan a routine task, carry it out, and report on it. The task is to fit a surface switch box and a surface socket-outlet box on the Centre's practice board and connect a switch and a socket outlet to the cables the assessor has run. The board is NOT connected to any supply at any time. Stage 1, plan (about 45 minutes): together, fill in a short job sheet with the steps in order, the tools and materials, the hazards and controls, and a time for each step, and agree who does each step. Stage 2, toolbox talk (about 10 minutes): one member leads a short talk on the plan and its hazards, while the others ask questions. Stage 3, carry out (about 1 hour 30 minutes): follow the plan, with every member doing at least one step at the board while another member checks it against the job sheet. Note the actual time of each step. Stage 4, check and report (about 30 minutes): check the finished work against the job sheet, then fill in a job completion report: what was done, the materials used, planned and actual times, any problems, and what the group would plan differently next time. Each member says one thing they learned. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in the job sheet and report once for the whole group.
materials: Practice board with cables already run by the assessor, not connected to any supply
A surface switch box and a surface socket-outlet box, a switch and a socket outlet, and fixing screws
Electrician's hand tools and a cordless drill
A job sheet and a job completion report form
A clock or phone to note the times
Safety glasses and safety boots for every member
A phone or camera for the photos
photos: The completed job sheet, with steps, materials, hazards and times
The toolbox talk, with the job sheet in view
Tools and materials laid out and checked against the job sheet
The boxes fixed on the board
The switch and socket outlet connected and fitted straight
The finished work being checked against the job sheet
The completed job report and the cleaned work area
checklist: Took part in writing the job sheet, with steps in a sensible order
Took part in the toolbox talk and asked or answered a question
Carried out their step as planned, safely and neatly
Checked another member's step against the job sheet
Noted the actual time and any problems
Helped fill in the job report, including what to plan differently
Cleaned up and returned the tools and unused materials
safety: The practice board must not be connected to any supply at any time during this task
Wear safety glasses when drilling and stripping cables
Check each tool before use and keep the floor clear of off-cuts
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
